sources.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.” - MIT Technology Review
passages: Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone .
The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario?
“All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper.

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.
In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia.

extraction.body: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing? What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log. Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning. “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it. Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore. Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.” “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations. “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. passages: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.

Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.

Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.

Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.

AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.

“There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed.

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.

Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”

As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.)

Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.”

Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.

“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.”

Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”

“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.”

As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.

“There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.”

“Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

extraction.body: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. “We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.” “Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt. The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring.” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.” When the game reset and ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround, that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring. Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote. The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told MIT Tech Review she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said. The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings Anthony Ha Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept Connie Loizos

extraction.body: With no assigned goals, AI agents created their own challenges — and learned from them. What happens when you put an AI on a virtual deserted island, all alone with no task or objective? Apparently, it finds things to do by itself. MIT researchers were amazed to see a lone figure carrying a ring to the top of a ridge, place it on the ground like a basketball hoop, and begin taking shots with a block. The figure was an artificial intelligence called Eko, operating a virtual avatar through written commands that it gave. Nobody had told it to play basketball. In fact, nobody had given it any particular task at all. But Eko was finding plenty of ways to entertain itself. It invented bowling, built elaborate sculptures, and experimented with the strange physics of its little world. At one point, it discovered that throwing a particular rock hard enough caused new building blocks to appear, a hidden feature the researchers had programmed into the simulation. Eko exploited the discovery to create increasingly elaborate arrangements, eventually recreating constellations on the ground. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” it wrote in its activity log. These curious antics were part of an experiment at MIT exploring the rather wild idea whether an artificial intelligence can learn through play, much as children and animals do. In a new study , researchers placed 13 independent AI agents on the same simulated island for 30 hours each. Without assignments, scores or rewards, the agents invented their own challenges, investigated their surroundings and developed skills that later made them better at solving problems. Please check your inbox and confirm your subscription. The researchers conclude that aimless exploration might offer a powerful new way to teach AI, although whether the machines were truly ‘playing’ remains an open question. The island was sparse, comprising a few raised platforms, 12 cubes, a rock and a ring. Eko could move, jump, pick up objects and throw them. It never saw pictures, only textual descriptions of coordinates and objects. One agent positioned the ring as a basketball hoop. Another arranged cubes like bowling pins. After hurling its ring into the ocean, Eko built a heart-shaped memorial. A different agent canceled its own 50-catch juggling record after realizing the objects had barely left its grasp, then tried again under stricter rules. The researchers at MIT believe the AI agents are essentially playing. They base their judgment on four hallmarks of animal and human play, which the AI also exhibited. These are inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, pretending objects were something else and pursuing activities without an outside payoff. “This is playing,” Antonio Norelli, an MIT researcher and coauthor, told MIT Technology Review . “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” The real test, however, was what happened afterward. To find out whether all this playing had taught the agents anything useful, the researchers gave them actual jobs. They compared the 13 agents that had spent 30 hours exploring the island with 13 fresh copies that had never been there before. One challenge was to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak within an hour. The experienced agents managed an average of 10.3 objects, while the newcomers managed just 3.5. The experienced agents also generally performed better at other tasks, including building multiple towers out of blocks. But how had they learned? The AI itself hadn’t been retrained. Instead, the agents had spent their time on the island keeping detailed notes about what worked, what failed, and which tricks they had discovered. These notes survived even when the simulation reset, allowing the agents to build on their previous experiences. To test whether those logged activities really amounted to anything, the researchers deliberately erased specific discoveries from the agents’ notes. For instance, one agent had learned that throwing a rock could generate extra building blocks. When researchers deleted that knowledge, the agent went from building an average of six towers to just two. The experiment showed that Eko wasn’t merely acting playful. It was acquiring practical knowledge that helped it solve new problems. There was a catch, however. The agents sometimes learned the wrong lessons. One had mistakenly concluded that stacking blocks directly didn’t work well. When researchers erased that false belief from its memory, it actually became better at building towers. Like a student who had misunderstood a lesson, Eko could carry its mistakes into future challenges. Other projects have pursued open-ended learning, including an agent named Voyager, which learned skills in Minecraft , and Google DeepMind’s XLand . But they used automatically generated objectives or rewards. Eko’s activities arose without a specific task or scoring system telling it what to practice. Yet the behavior was not entirely unprompted. Its initial instructions described it as naturally curious and fond of exploration, and automated messages repeatedly urged it to continue. Five agents deprived of that persona still displayed a comparable range of activities, although trials using two other AI systems produced narrower behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review . She cautioned that the agents might simply be imitating human play, perhaps due to some subtle conditioning in the agent’s system prompt. And it’s not just play. The experiments reported some useful learning. For instance, some agents discovered that jumping before throwing could launch blocks far higher, a trick even the simulator’s designers had overlooked. The approach could help robots cope with unfamiliar environments. But researchers warn that autonomous exploration belongs in controlled playgrounds, not uncontrolled real-world settings. A different agent canceled its own 50-catch juggling record after realizing the objects had barely left its grasp, then tried again under stricter rules.

The researchers at MIT believe the AI agents are essentially playing. They base their judgment on four hallmarks of animal and human play, which the AI also exhibited. These are inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, pretending objects were something else and pursuing activities without an outside payoff.
“This is playing,” Antonio Norelli, an MIT researcher and coauthor, told MIT Technology Review . “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”
The real test, however, was what happened afterward.

To find out whether all this playing had taught the agents anything useful, the researchers gave them actual jobs. They compared the 13 agents that had spent 30 hours exploring the island with 13 fresh copies that had never been there before.

One challenge was to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak within an hour. The experienced agents managed an average of 10.3 objects, while the newcomers managed just 3.5. The experienced agents also generally performed better at other tasks, including building multiple towers out of blocks.

But how had they learned? The AI itself hadn’t been retrained. Instead, the agents had spent their time on the island keeping detailed notes about what worked, what failed, and which tricks they had discovered. These notes survived even when the simulation reset, allowing the agents to build on their previous experiences.

To test whether those logged activities really amounted to anything, the researchers deliberately erased specific discoveries from the agents’ notes. For instance, one agent had learned that throwing a rock could generate extra building blocks. When researchers deleted that knowledge, the agent went from building an average of six towers to just two. The experiment showed that Eko wasn’t merely acting playful. It was acquiring practical knowledge that helped it solve new problems.

There was a catch, however. The agents sometimes learned the wrong lessons. One had mistakenly concluded that stacking blocks directly didn’t work well. When researchers erased that false belief from its memory, it actually became better at building towers. Like a student who had misunderstood a lesson, Eko could carry its mistakes into future challenges.

Other projects have pursued open-ended learning, including an agent named Voyager, which learned skills in Minecraft , and Google DeepMind’s XLand . But they used automatically generated objectives or rewards. Eko’s activities arose without a specific task or scoring system telling it what to practice.

Yet the behavior was not entirely unprompted. Its initial instructions described it as naturally curious and fond of exploration, and automated messages repeatedly urged it to continue. Five agents deprived of that persona still displayed a comparable range of activities, although trials using two other AI systems produced narrower behavior.

“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review . She cautioned that the agents might simply be imitating human play, perhaps due to some subtle conditioning in the agent’s system prompt.

And it’s not just play. The experiments reported some useful learning. For instance, some agents discovered that jumping before throwing could launch blocks far higher, a trick even the simulator’s designers had overlooked.
The approach could help robots cope with unfamiliar environments. But researchers warn that autonomous exploration belongs in controlled playgrounds, not uncontrolled real-world settings.

coreStoryFacts.text: Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone .
The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario?
“All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper.

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.
In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia.
The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours.
The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.
AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own.
“Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.”

What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.

Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.

Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.

Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.

AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.

“There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed.

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.

Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”

As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.)

Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.”

Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.

“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.”

Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”

“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.”

As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.

“There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.”

“Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. “We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.” “Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt. The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. extraction.body: With no assigned goals, AI agents created their own challenges — and learned from them. What happens when you put an AI on a virtual deserted island, all alone with no task or objective? Apparently, it finds things to do by itself. MIT researchers were amazed to see a lone figure carrying a ring to the top of a ridge, place it on the ground like a basketball hoop, and begin taking shots with a block. The figure was an artificial intelligence called Eko, operating a virtual avatar through written commands that it gave. Nobody had told it to play basketball. In fact, nobody had given it any particular task at all. But Eko was finding plenty of ways to entertain itself. It invented bowling, built elaborate sculptures, and experimented with the strange physics of its little world. At one point, it discovered that throwing a particular rock hard enough caused new building blocks to appear, a hidden feature the researchers had programmed into the simulation. Eko exploited the discovery to create increasingly elaborate arrangements, eventually recreating constellations on the ground. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” it wrote in its activity log. These curious antics were part of an experiment at MIT exploring the rather wild idea whether an artificial intelligence can learn through play, much as children and animals do. In a new study , researchers placed 13 independent AI agents on the same simulated island for 30 hours each. Without assignments, scores or rewards, the agents invented their own challenges, investigated their surroundings and developed skills that later made them better at solving problems. Please check your inbox and confirm your subscription. The researchers conclude that aimless exploration might offer a powerful new way to teach AI, although whether the machines were truly ‘playing’ remains an open question. The island was sparse, comprising a few raised platforms, 12 cubes, a rock and a ring. Eko could move, jump, pick up objects and throw them. It never saw pictures, only textual descriptions of coordinates and objects. One agent positioned the ring as a basketball hoop. Another arranged cubes like bowling pins. After hurling its ring into the ocean, Eko built a heart-shaped memorial. A different agent canceled its own 50-catch juggling record after realizing the objects had barely left its grasp, then tried again under stricter rules. The researchers at MIT believe the AI agents are essentially playing. They base their judgment on four hallmarks of animal and human play, which the AI also exhibited. These are inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, pretending objects were something else and pursuing activities without an outside payoff. “This is playing,” Antonio Norelli, an MIT researcher and coauthor, told MIT Technology Review . “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” The real test, however, was what happened afterward. To find out whether all this playing had taught the agents anything useful, the researchers gave them actual jobs. They compared the 13 agents that had spent 30 hours exploring the island with 13 fresh copies that had never been there before. One challenge was to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak within an hour. The experienced agents managed an average of 10.3 objects, while the newcomers managed just 3.5. The experienced agents also generally performed better at other tasks, including building multiple towers out of blocks. But how had they learned? The AI itself hadn’t been retrained. Instead, the agents had spent their time on the island keeping detailed notes about what worked, what failed, and which tricks they had discovered. These notes survived even when the simulation reset, allowing the agents to build on their previous experiences. To test whether those logged activities really amounted to anything, the researchers deliberately erased specific discoveries from the agents’ notes. For instance, one agent had learned that throwing a rock could generate extra building blocks. When researchers deleted that knowledge, the agent went from building an average of six towers to just two. The experiment showed that Eko wasn’t merely acting playful. It was acquiring practical knowledge that helped it solve new problems. There was a catch, however. The agents sometimes learned the wrong lessons. One had mistakenly concluded that stacking blocks directly didn’t work well. When researchers erased that false belief from its memory, it actually became better at building towers. Like a student who had misunderstood a lesson, Eko could carry its mistakes into future challenges. Other projects have pursued open-ended learning, including an agent named Voyager, which learned skills in Minecraft , and Google DeepMind’s XLand . But they used automatically generated objectives or rewards. Eko’s activities arose without a specific task or scoring system telling it what to practice. Yet the behavior was not entirely unprompted. Its initial instructions described it as naturally curious and fond of exploration, and automated messages repeatedly urged it to continue. Five agents deprived of that persona still displayed a comparable range of activities, although trials using two other AI systems produced narrower behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review . She cautioned that the agents might simply be imitating human play, perhaps due to some subtle conditioning in the agent’s system prompt. And it’s not just play. The experiments reported some useful learning. For instance, some agents discovered that jumping before throwing could launch blocks far higher, a trick even the simulator’s designers had overlooked. The approach could help robots cope with unfamiliar environments. But researchers warn that autonomous exploration belongs in controlled playgrounds, not uncontrolled real-world settings. The experienced agents also generally performed better at other tasks, including building multiple towers out of blocks.

But how had they learned? The AI itself hadn’t been retrained. Instead, the agents had spent their time on the island keeping detailed notes about what worked, what failed, and which tricks they had discovered. These notes survived even when the simulation reset, allowing the agents to build on their previous experiences.

To test whether those logged activities really amounted to anything, the researchers deliberately erased specific discoveries from the agents’ notes. For instance, one agent had learned that throwing a rock could generate extra building blocks. When researchers deleted that knowledge, the agent went from building an average of six towers to just two. The experiment showed that Eko wasn’t merely acting playful. It was acquiring practical knowledge that helped it solve new problems.

There was a catch, however. The agents sometimes learned the wrong lessons. One had mistakenly concluded that stacking blocks directly didn’t work well. When researchers erased that false belief from its memory, it actually became better at building towers. Like a student who had misunderstood a lesson, Eko could carry its mistakes into future challenges.

Other projects have pursued open-ended learning, including an agent named Voyager, which learned skills in Minecraft , and Google DeepMind’s XLand . But they used automatically generated objectives or rewards. Eko’s activities arose without a specific task or scoring system telling it what to practice.

Yet the behavior was not entirely unprompted. Its initial instructions described it as naturally curious and fond of exploration, and automated messages repeatedly urged it to continue. Five agents deprived of that persona still displayed a comparable range of activities, although trials using two other AI systems produced narrower behavior.

“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review . She cautioned that the agents might simply be imitating human play, perhaps due to some subtle conditioning in the agent’s system prompt.

And it’s not just play. The experiments reported some useful learning. For instance, some agents discovered that jumping before throwing could launch blocks far higher, a trick even the simulator’s designers had overlooked.
The approach could help robots cope with unfamiliar environments. But researchers warn that autonomous exploration belongs in controlled playgrounds, not uncontrolled real-world settings.

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: AI agents tend to do things when we give them specific commands, such as analyzing data and answering questions. But what would they do if left to their own devices? That's what researchers from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) wanted to find out when they stranded several agents on a virtual desert island and left them without any specific tasks to complete. There were 13 agents in total, all named Eko, which were built using the AI coding assistant Claude Code. Each was given a virtual body and text files to record their memories and discoveries and left alone on their own copy of Mesa World. This was a simulated 3D island built on a custom game engine called Clawblox. The agents stayed on their islands for 30 hours, during which time they received no specific tasks or directions from humans about what activities to pursue. They were simply instructed to be curious and eager to explore. They could not visualize the island, so instead received text descriptions of where objects were and controlled their virtual bodies by typing basic commands like jump, pick up or throw. To keep the AI from running out of short-term memory, the island was restored to its original state every hour, and the AI's current session was reset. However, the agents did not lose their recorded knowledge and discoveries, because they could write notes, guides and discoveries into text files that survived each hourly reset. While the agents roamed their virtual world, the researchers recorded and analyzed their behavior. What they observed is detailed in a new paper posted on the arXiv preprint server. Instead of freezing or repeating the same basic action over and over, which you might expect when an AI isn't given any specific tasks, the agents were surprisingly creative. Without any human prompting, they built complex towers, arranged geometric ground patterns and even improvised their own versions of bowling, basketball and juggling. In other words, they were displaying behaviors that resembled play. The researchers reached this conclusion after evaluating the agents' actions against four classic signatures of play. These are inventing their own rules, repeating activities with variations, engaging in make-believe and pursuing goals that appeared to be for their own sake. For instance, the AI created its own arbitrary challenges, like hopping across blocks without touching the ground, and transformed simple props, using a ring as a basketball hoop. But this playtime wasn't just for fun. It helped them learn. Agents that had spent 30 hours on their island generally performed better on later tasks than newbie castaways. They learned techniques for building towers and placing objects on high platforms and even uncovered physics tricks that the creators hadn't realized their simulator allowed. "The agents' self-initiated exploration thus produced not only knowledge we had hidden for them to find, but knowledge of the world that its designers lacked," wrote the study authors. Therefore, giving AI room to play may be one way future systems learn. "Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks. Others may need something closer to a childhood." sources.title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
passages: The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.
Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google.
In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it.
The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs.
You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios.
Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus.

extraction.body: Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms. Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image. The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts. That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers . Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP. Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control. In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai . It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model. Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon. The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year . However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026 , causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion , according to external analysts.

coreStoryFacts.text: The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.
Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google.
In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it.
The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs.
You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios.
Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus.

The model will also be available through the Canva API.
It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.

extraction.body: Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms. Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image. The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts. That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers . Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP. Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control. In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai . It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model. Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon. The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year . However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026 , causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion , according to external analysts.

sources.title: 1Password now lets Claude sign in to websites without seeing your passwords - 9to5Mac
passages: 1Password is launching a new Claude integration for Mac users today.
It’s designed to let Anthropic’s AI agent sign in to websites without seeing your password or two-factor authentication code.
1Password can also broker access across multiple websites during the same task, allowing Claude to complete a multi-step workflow without stopping for a new login each time.
According to 1Password, approved credentials are delivered through a secure channel and injected directly into the destination page.
The password, one-time code, and other secrets never enter Claude’s context, memory, or Anthropic’s systems.
This is useful for things like booking travel or managing online accounts.
The Anthropic partnership was first outlined in March , when 1Password said Claude would gain consent-based access to vault items.
1Password for Claude is available now to Mac users on business, family, and individual plans.
It requires the 1Password desktop app and browser extension, along with the Claude desktop app and browser extension.
Instead of granting ongoing access to a vault, Claude requests the specific login items it needs for a task.
The user can approve or deny that request with a biometric prompt, and the permission lasts only for the current session.
When a compatible AI agent takes control of the browser, the 1Password extension automatically locks down the vault so that only the credentials explicitly approved for that task remain available.

sources.title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
passages: Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.

“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”

extraction.body: Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. coreStoryFacts.text: 1Password is launching a new Claude integration for Mac users today.
It’s designed to let Anthropic’s AI agent sign in to websites without seeing your password or two-factor authentication code.
1Password can also broker access across multiple websites during the same task, allowing Claude to complete a multi-step workflow without stopping for a new login each time.
According to 1Password, approved credentials are delivered through a secure channel and injected directly into the destination page.
The password, one-time code, and other secrets never enter Claude’s context, memory, or Anthropic’s systems.
This is useful for things like booking travel or managing online accounts.
The Anthropic partnership was first outlined in March , when 1Password said Claude would gain consent-based access to vault items.
1Password for Claude is available now to Mac users on business, family, and individual plans.
It requires the 1Password desktop app and browser extension, along with the Claude desktop app and browser extension.
Instead of granting ongoing access to a vault, Claude requests the specific login items it needs for a task.
The user can approve or deny that request with a biometric prompt, and the permission lasts only for the current session.
When a compatible AI agent takes control of the browser, the 1Password extension automatically locks down the vault so that only the credentials explicitly approved for that task remain available.

Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.

“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”

1Password also said the process keeps the credential out of the agent’s view, and it removes the credential so the agent cannot read or reuse it as it continues the task.

Access is per-session and requires user approval for each sign-in request.

extraction.body: Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. relevantPassages.text: 1Password launched 1Password for Agents, a sign-in platform that lets personal AI agents log into accounts without ever seeing or storing users’ passwords.

1Password said the system works by sending a unique digital key to 1Password when an agent reaches a login page, and 1Password then fills the required information into the sign-in form after the user approves.
1Password also said the process keeps the credential out of the agent’s view, and it removes the credential so the agent cannot read or reuse it as it continues the task.
Most outlets agree 1Password lets agents sign in without seeing passwords, using per-request approval and agent identity keys.
Access is per-session and requires user approval for each sign-in request.
1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
TechCrunch tied the timing to broader concerns about agentic activity, noting that Axios reported that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.

Aashish Tripathi, 1Password’s chief product officer, said, "An agent should be able to do the job it's been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account." John Torrey, 1Password’s chief business officer, said, "a safe way to let agents do the work without handing over their passwords."

extraction.body: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems. Developers of the PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. They said around 1345 GMT on Wednesday that a new version fixing the vulnerabilities was live. But with reports that hackers were exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline ahead of the fix as a precaution. PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack. "PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post. Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare , said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure. "We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update," he said on X. Wordfence, a security plugin that protects WordPress websites, said all WordPress sites run on a PHP-installed server. It warned that automatic updates would not apply the fix and advised site owners to find out who is responsible for updating PHP on their sites. Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. Officials have said that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not yet disclosed which versions are vulnerable. PHP is a programming language used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers. It is also among the most widely used software on the internet. PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs. It is the engine behind WordPress, which powers about 43% of all websites from blogs and small business pages to government portals, online stores and news sites. Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, said: "We don't comment on the details of security issues, but our team is prepared and has been working with the PHP security team to ensure a smooth update." Security experts said the vulnerabilities could potentially open the door to millions of servers because so many websites rely on the same underlying software. Rather than target victims individually, attackers could scan the internet for systems running vulnerable versions of PHP. AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have proliferated in recent weeks, could magnify the threat, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London. "The scale is huge," Olejnik said. "And with AI exploitation may happen instantly, on a large scale." The risk is particularly acute for small websites run by individuals or organizations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly manage the underlying servers. Security experts said such sites could take longer to patch and remain exposed well after fixes become available. In the Netherlands, several organizations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Center and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national soccer association KNVB, the websites the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites. Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform, a spokesperson told Reuters. Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure." France's Interior Ministry said it had temporarily taken local government administrative websites offline while awaiting a security fix. extraction.body: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline yesterday (21 October) after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems. Developers of the PHP programming language yesterday released urgent fixes for vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years before being uncovered using AI, saying all users were "encouraged to update immediately". With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took websites offline as a precaution. Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools can reverse-engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers rushed to exploit the flaws before systems were updated. AI was powering a "race to exploit", said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet". PHP, a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page", underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is built into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability could have enormous knock-on consequences. "All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable," said Tiffany Farriss, interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. "This issue impacts the majority of the internet." Cybersecurity agencies around the world have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. According to data from Censys, the internet intelligence firm, about 1.5 million out of 2.6 million hosts report running a version of PHP for which there is no fix. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia also said it had taken an unspecified number of systems offline until they could be safely patched, while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it had also briefly gone offline to address the issue. Even some world leaders weighed in. The Dutch prime minister said he was closely monitoring the situation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a post on X that website owners should "check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix". The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, two cybersecurity companies said in independent reports. Calif said in a blog post that it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on 1 August and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it had also discovered the flaw with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to exploit, Wiz's post said. "Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale," it said. "With AI, this is no longer a barrier." Calif and Wiz said they had coordinated with one another, the PHP team and OpenAI on the discovery. In a statement, the White House said it had been made aware of the flaw on Friday. In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said the tech giant's security team had detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy "honeypot" systems on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding that it was unclear how the actor had learnt of the flaws while they were under embargo. More attempts followed on Wednesday by multiple actors before the embargo was lifted. Amazon said it was still unclear whether any of the attempts would have worked against real websites, adding that the flaws were "now being broadly exploited in the wild". Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline yesterday (21 October) after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, two cybersecurity companies said in independent reports.

In the Netherlands, several organisations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites of the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites.
