extraction.body: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline yesterday (21 October) after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems. Developers of the PHP programming language yesterday released urgent fixes for vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years before being uncovered using AI, saying all users were "encouraged to update immediately". With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took websites offline as a precaution. Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools can reverse-engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers rushed to exploit the flaws before systems were updated. AI was powering a "race to exploit", said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet". PHP, a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page", underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is built into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability could have enormous knock-on consequences. "All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable," said Tiffany Farriss, interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. "This issue impacts the majority of the internet." Cybersecurity agencies around the world have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. According to data from Censys, the internet intelligence firm, about 1.5 million out of 2.6 million hosts report running a version of PHP for which there is no fix. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia also said it had taken an unspecified number of systems offline until they could be safely patched, while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it had also briefly gone offline to address the issue. Even some world leaders weighed in. The Dutch prime minister said he was closely monitoring the situation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a post on X that website owners should "check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix". The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, two cybersecurity companies said in independent reports. Calif said in a blog post that it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on 1 August and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it had also discovered the flaw with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to exploit, Wiz's post said. "Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale," it said. "With AI, this is no longer a barrier." Calif and Wiz said they had coordinated with one another, the PHP team and OpenAI on the discovery. In a statement, the White House said it had been made aware of the flaw on Friday. In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said the tech giant's security team had detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy "honeypot" systems on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding that it was unclear how the actor had learnt of the flaws while they were under embargo. More attempts followed on Wednesday by multiple actors before the embargo was lifted. Amazon said it was still unclear whether any of the attempts would have worked against real websites, adding that the flaws were "now being broadly exploited in the wild". PHP is a programming language used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers. Its ubiquity, with PHP running roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs, has made experts anxious. AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have proliferated in recent weeks, could wreak havoc on unpatched servers, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London. "The scale is huge, and with AI, exploitation may happen instantly," Olejnik said. WordPress.com operator Automattic said users of its hosted solutions and Tumblr were safe from the bug. Risks were higher for small PHP-powered websites run by individuals or organisations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly manage the underlying servers. In the Netherlands, several organisations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites of the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites. Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform. Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure". France's Interior Ministry said it had placed all its websites into preventive maintenance. extraction.body: He wears the camera for five or six hours a day. "It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim. He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities. Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work. That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world. Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data. "Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig. His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work. "For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says. Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says. "We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off." And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year. Shahil Baig expects dozens more firms to start collecting video of workers And until recently, that data was not available. "There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco. At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia. The factory workers teaching robots how to work like humans But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs? At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai. For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says. The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about. "By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says. Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI. Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development. Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day. Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years. "Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says. He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work. "It doesn't cost me anything. I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting. Now I just get paid a little more for it," he says. Mohammed Arman has been filming his tailoring work While there is demand for such footage it will be collected somewhere. "India can't afford to stay a footage supplier. It needs to move up the value chain: from recording raw video to owning the pipeline that turns that video into something usable - cleaning it, structuring it, validating it, and ultimately setting the standards for what counts as high-quality training data," he says. Jolly Arifur has been filming domestic work for a few hours a day For some people collecting data is attractive part time work. Science teacher Jolly Arifur was looking for work she could do from home that would fit around her young son. "For the past seven months, I strapped a rig-mounted camera on my head while doing my routine domestic work scrubbing, cooking, sweeping tile floors, and folding laundry."

With that in mind, there's one name that I've already circled for a potential major rebound next year: Cardano (CRYPTO: ADA). Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Just five years ago, Cardano ranked as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency on the planet, trailing only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB . At the time, Cardano had a market cap of $70 billion, and appeared to have a path to toppling Ethereum as the world's premier Layer-1 blockchain network. But that never happened. Down another 40% in 2026, Cardano now trades for a bargain-basement price of just $0.21. Its market cap has slid to less than $8 billion. In fact, Cardano's fall has been so precipitous that it has already dropped out of the list of the top 10 cryptocurrencies (as measured by market cap). But a few factors are working in Cardano's favor right now. One of these is a renewed emphasis on decentralized finance (DeFi). At the beginning of the year, the Cardano developer community released a far-reaching strategy document ("Cardano 2030 Strategic Framework") with details on how they planned to turn things around in DeFi. And they gave very specific goals for user growth, transaction activity, and market share gains. That might sound like pie-in-the-sky thinking, except for one fact: Cardano co-founder Charles Hoskinson is also one of the co-founders of Ethereum and knows a thing or two about putting together a world-class blockchain network. Hoskinson is currently working on a new programming language for the Cardano blockchain platform, and that could mean big things ahead if it opens up new opportunities in fast-growing areas such as artificial intelligence. If Cardano can turn things around next year, a good template could be Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), which saw a monster turnaround after losing 94% of its value in 2022. The following year, Solana soared by 924% as investors realized that it had been oversold amid broader fears of a full-fledged crypto meltdown. Like Solana, Cardano is a Layer-1 smart contract platform. And, similar to Solana several years ago, Cardano is currently trading at a massive discount to its all-time high. In 2027, there is one type of altcoin that I'm expecting to perform particularly well: beaten-down cryptocurrencies that have pretty much been left for dead in 2026. With that in mind, there's one name that I've already circled for a potential major rebound next year: Cardano (CRYPTO: ADA).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Just five years ago, Cardano ranked as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency on the planet, trailing only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB . At the time, Cardano had a market cap of $70 billion, and appeared to have a path to toppling Ethereum as the world's premier Layer-1 blockchain network.

But that never happened. Down another 40% in 2026, Cardano now trades for a bargain-basement price of just $0.21. Its market cap has slid to less than $8 billion. In fact, Cardano's fall has been so precipitous that it has already dropped out of the list of the top 10 cryptocurrencies (as measured by market cap).
But a few factors are working in Cardano's favor right now.

One of these is a renewed emphasis on decentralized finance (DeFi). At the beginning of the year, the Cardano developer community released a far-reaching strategy document ("Cardano 2030 Strategic Framework") with details on how they planned to turn things around in DeFi. And they gave very specific goals for user growth, transaction activity, and market share gains.

That might sound like pie-in-the-sky thinking, except for one fact: Cardano co-founder Charles Hoskinson is also one of the co-founders of Ethereum and knows a thing or two about putting together a world-class blockchain network.

Hoskinson is currently working on a new programming language for the Cardano blockchain platform, and that could mean big things ahead if it opens up new opportunities in fast-growing areas such as artificial intelligence.

If Cardano can turn things around next year, a good template could be Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), which saw a monster turnaround after losing 94% of its value in 2022. The following year, Solana soared by 924% as investors realized that it had been oversold amid broader fears of a full-fledged crypto meltdown.
Like Solana, Cardano is a Layer-1 smart contract platform. And, similar to Solana several years ago, Cardano is currently trading at a massive discount to its all-time high.

This is not to say that Cardano will 10x in 2027. But I wouldn't be surprised at all if it climbs back past the $1 mark. As recently as January 2025, Cardano traded for $1. That's nearly a 5x return, and much higher than Bitcoin or Ethereum is projected to return. It's a risky bet, of course, but at a price of just $0.21, Cardano is just too cheap to ignore.

sources.title: Wall Street's Biggest Settlement Firm Is Lining Up Stellar for 2027. Is XLM a Better Buy Than Ethereum? - 24/7 Wall St.
passages: Wall Street's biggest settlement firm just named Stellar as a future partner, sending XLM back onto traders' watchlists.
But before you chase the catalyst, the comparison with Ethereum reveals some uncomfortable truths about timing, tokenization dominance, and price reality.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10.
If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days.
Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground.
In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization.
Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap.
Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain.
Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry.
Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins.
However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure.
XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours.

But before you chase the catalyst, the comparison with Ethereum reveals some uncomfortable truths about timing, tokenization dominance, and price reality. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap. Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. With this news, XLM is back on buyers’ radar, especially after a 15.3% decline over the past two weeks. XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours. By comparison, Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) trades around $2,417 and plays a major role in the tokenized asset market, though its connection to DTCC’s upcoming service is less direct. So, in the XLM vs Ethereum debate, which cryptocurrency stands as the better investment to capitalize on the tokenization trend? The initial rollout will cover 25 stocks, ETFs, and U.S. Treasuries, with each token fully backed by a corresponding security held at the Depository Trust Company (DTC), a DTCC subsidiary. Token holders will have the flexibility to transfer their tokens at any time between registered wallets. DTCC estimates it will have around $30 trillion in assets available for tokenization. Before the official launch, DTCC conducted a successful test on July 15, turning DTC-held securities into tokens for live trades on both Besu and Canton, involving more than 30 participating firms. DTCC has described this initiative as part of a “multi-chain strategy” to ensure resiliency, scalability, and choice for users. While DTCC’s roadmap indicates a potential inclusion for Stellar and the Arc network in 2027, this plan is subject to change. Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry. Stellar has already made strides in this space, managing $3.6 billion in tokenized real-world assets (excluding stablecoins), ranking fourth among all networks, according to rwa.xyz data from October 17. These real-world assets (RWAs) include tokenized Treasury funds and private credit. However, despite its accomplishments, XLM’s price does not reflect this progress well. XLM trades 79.6% below its January 2018 peak of $0.88 and has fallen 41.4% over the past year. XLM’s supply also puts pressure on its price. Approximately 35.2 billion of 50 billion XLM tokens are in circulation, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all tokens were in circulation) of about $8.9 billion, compared with a market cap of around $6.3 billion. This indicates that more tokens could be released into the market, potentially absorbing new demand. The connection between Ethereum and DTCC comes through Besu, an Ethereum client, meaning DTCC’s private network uses Ethereum technology but operates separately from the public Ethereum blockchain. Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins. In contrast, Stellar holds only $535 million in stablecoins, according to the same data source. Price performance has also favored Ethereum. ETH trades 51.1% below its record high of $4,946 from August 2025 and is up 29.3% over the past 90 days, while XLM has dropped 3.8%. Over the last two weeks, ETH fell 9.3% , while XLM fell more sharply, down 15.3%. One advantage XLM has is its smaller market cap, with Ethereum’s $295.2 billion about 47 times larger. Smaller cryptocurrencies can often react more sharply to news from large partners. However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure. In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization. DTCC’s 2027 roadmap doesn’t change that. Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change. For XLM to narrow the gap, DTCC’s October launch needs to progress smoothly, Stellar’s rollout date must be confirmed, and its tokenized asset base should keep growing. Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10. If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days. Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground. Stellar just cracked the top three blockchains for tokenized real-world assets, and XLM's price jumped the same week. But the connection between those two facts is far more complicated than it looks. XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) and Stellar (CRYPTO: XLM) were both built to solve the same remittance problem. International payments are slow, expensive, and routed through a chain of correspondent banks that each add delays and… XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) and Stellar have always been chasing the same prize, which is moving money and assets across borders without the old banking rails. XRP is far the bigger of the two, worth tens… Stellar just landed partnerships with a major US bank, the DTCC, and two federal regulators in a single month, yet XLM still trades far below a key resistance level that has blocked every rally… Stellar just crossed a technical threshold that XRP is still struggling to reach, but a surge in ETF inflows could flip the script heading into Q4. These two payments coins are telling very different… Stellar hosts more tokenized real-world assets than the XRP Ledger, yet XLM trades at a fraction of XRP's price. The reason comes down to a structural flaw in how Stellar's tokenization boom actually works. This move showcases the growing trend of tokenization, which has found increasing popularity as a new way to represent the ownership rights of real-world assets as digital tokens on a blockchain. XRP and Ethereum both sit far below their 2025 peaks, and the path back looks very different for each coin. ETF flows, banking partnerships, and upcoming upgrades will determine which one gets there first. With that in mind, there's one name that I've already circled for a potential major rebound next year: Cardano (CRYPTO: ADA). Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Just five years ago, Cardano ranked as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency on the planet, trailing only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB . At the time, Cardano had a market cap of $70 billion, and appeared to have a path to toppling Ethereum as the world's premier Layer-1 blockchain network. But that never happened. Down another 40% in 2026, Cardano now trades for a bargain-basement price of just $0.21. Its market cap has slid to less than $8 billion. In fact, Cardano's fall has been so precipitous that it has already dropped out of the list of the top 10 cryptocurrencies (as measured by market cap). But a few factors are working in Cardano's favor right now. One of these is a renewed emphasis on decentralized finance (DeFi). At the beginning of the year, the Cardano developer community released a far-reaching strategy document ("Cardano 2030 Strategic Framework") with details on how they planned to turn things around in DeFi. And they gave very specific goals for user growth, transaction activity, and market share gains. That might sound like pie-in-the-sky thinking, except for one fact: Cardano co-founder Charles Hoskinson is also one of the co-founders of Ethereum and knows a thing or two about putting together a world-class blockchain network. Hoskinson is currently working on a new programming language for the Cardano blockchain platform, and that could mean big things ahead if it opens up new opportunities in fast-growing areas such as artificial intelligence. If Cardano can turn things around next year, a good template could be Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), which saw a monster turnaround after losing 94% of its value in 2022. The following year, Solana soared by 924% as investors realized that it had been oversold amid broader fears of a full-fledged crypto meltdown. Like Solana, Cardano is a Layer-1 smart contract platform. And, similar to Solana several years ago, Cardano is currently trading at a massive discount to its all-time high. passages: Wall Street's biggest settlement firm just named Stellar as a future partner, sending XLM back onto traders' watchlists.
But before you chase the catalyst, the comparison with Ethereum reveals some uncomfortable truths about timing, tokenization dominance, and price reality.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10.
If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days.
Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground.
In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization.
Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap.
Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain.
Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry.
Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins.
However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure.
XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap. Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. With this news, XLM is back on buyers’ radar, especially after a 15.3% decline over the past two weeks. XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours. By comparison, Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) trades around $2,417 and plays a major role in the tokenized asset market, though its connection to DTCC’s upcoming service is less direct. So, in the XLM vs Ethereum debate, which cryptocurrency stands as the better investment to capitalize on the tokenization trend? The initial rollout will cover 25 stocks, ETFs, and U.S. Treasuries, with each token fully backed by a corresponding security held at the Depository Trust Company (DTC), a DTCC subsidiary. Token holders will have the flexibility to transfer their tokens at any time between registered wallets. DTCC estimates it will have around $30 trillion in assets available for tokenization. Before the official launch, DTCC conducted a successful test on July 15, turning DTC-held securities into tokens for live trades on both Besu and Canton, involving more than 30 participating firms. DTCC has described this initiative as part of a “multi-chain strategy” to ensure resiliency, scalability, and choice for users. While DTCC’s roadmap indicates a potential inclusion for Stellar and the Arc network in 2027, this plan is subject to change. Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry. Stellar has already made strides in this space, managing $3.6 billion in tokenized real-world assets (excluding stablecoins), ranking fourth among all networks, according to rwa.xyz data from October 17. These real-world assets (RWAs) include tokenized Treasury funds and private credit. However, despite its accomplishments, XLM’s price does not reflect this progress well. XLM trades 79.6% below its January 2018 peak of $0.88 and has fallen 41.4% over the past year. XLM’s supply also puts pressure on its price. Approximately 35.2 billion of 50 billion XLM tokens are in circulation, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all tokens were in circulation) of about $8.9 billion, compared with a market cap of around $6.3 billion. This indicates that more tokens could be released into the market, potentially absorbing new demand. The connection between Ethereum and DTCC comes through Besu, an Ethereum client, meaning DTCC’s private network uses Ethereum technology but operates separately from the public Ethereum blockchain. Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins. In contrast, Stellar holds only $535 million in stablecoins, according to the same data source. Price performance has also favored Ethereum. ETH trades 51.1% below its record high of $4,946 from August 2025 and is up 29.3% over the past 90 days, while XLM has dropped 3.8%. Over the last two weeks, ETH fell 9.3% , while XLM fell more sharply, down 15.3%. One advantage XLM has is its smaller market cap, with Ethereum’s $295.2 billion about 47 times larger. Smaller cryptocurrencies can often react more sharply to news from large partners. However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure. In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization. DTCC’s 2027 roadmap doesn’t change that. Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change. For XLM to narrow the gap, DTCC’s October launch needs to progress smoothly, Stellar’s rollout date must be confirmed, and its tokenized asset base should keep growing. Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10. If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days. Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground. Stellar just cracked the top three blockchains for tokenized real-world assets, and XLM's price jumped the same week. But the connection between those two facts is far more complicated than it looks. XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) and Stellar (CRYPTO: XLM) were both built to solve the same remittance problem. International payments are slow, expensive, and routed through a chain of correspondent banks that each add delays and… XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) and Stellar have always been chasing the same prize, which is moving money and assets across borders without the old banking rails. XRP is far the bigger of the two, worth tens… Stellar just landed partnerships with a major US bank, the DTCC, and two federal regulators in a single month, yet XLM still trades far below a key resistance level that has blocked every rally… Stellar just crossed a technical threshold that XRP is still struggling to reach, but a surge in ETF inflows could flip the script heading into Q4. These two payments coins are telling very different… Stellar hosts more tokenized real-world assets than the XRP Ledger, yet XLM trades at a fraction of XRP's price. The reason comes down to a structural flaw in how Stellar's tokenization boom actually works. This move showcases the growing trend of tokenization, which has found increasing popularity as a new way to represent the ownership rights of real-world assets as digital tokens on a blockchain. XRP and Ethereum both sit far below their 2025 peaks, and the path back looks very different for each coin. ETF flows, banking partnerships, and upcoming upgrades will determine which one gets there first. extraction.body: This paper is part of a series published by the National Governors Association (NGA) to identify actions Governors can take to guide their states and territories through intentional and effective power sector transformations. This paper provides a deeper dive into actions Governors can take to modernize the grid through the deployment of grid technologies. Electric power grids in the United States are in a period of rapid transformation, driven by a confluence of factors such as an increase in electricity demand, retirement of certain baseload power generation, an increase in distributed generation, lengthy interconnection queues and new “grid-edge” technologies being brought online. Layered into this evolution are new state and national decarbonization objectives, heightened awareness of the magnitude and frequency of threats that could compromise reliable power delivery, and unprecedented federal investment through legislation like the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). With these transformative trends in process, Governors are eager to support deployment of technology solutions to facilitate their policy objectives and meet increased loads – and doing so while maintaining or even improving grid reliability, resilience and affordability. This paper is part of a series published by the National Governors Association (NGA) to identify actions Governors can take to guide their states and territories through intentional and effective power sector transformations. While other papers explore regulatory structures, regional markets and power transmission, this paper provides a deeper dive into actions Governors can take to modernize the grid through the deployment of grid technologies. While careful planning, stakeholder engagement and robust technical analysis is needed to optimize technology investment, an understanding of the range of technologies currently available can help Governors determine how best to initiate or improve those processes in their states and territories. Often a combination of technologies will best allow states and grid operators to meet their objectives. While by no means exhaustive, this paper will focus on several of the grid modernizing technologies that are commercially available and being deployed: Underpinning modernization of the electric grid are regulatory structures and robust planning processes that work to meet specific objectives, such as resilience, reliability, affordability or decarbonization. Strengthening these structures and approaching grid modernization from a comprehensive planning perspective will create an environment for sustained innovation within the electrical sector. Governors’ strategies to guide the deployment of grid modernizing technologies addressed in this paper include: The electrical grid of the United States supports all aspects of the economy, as well as the safety of all Americans. From powering homes, schools and businesses to critical infrastructure and industries, the safe, reliable and affordable flow of electricity is essential to modern life. The electric grids have evolved from a loosely connected set of systems to a vast network of interconnected infrastructure serving hundreds of millions of customers. The electrical grid is undergoing a robust transformation, driven by (1) an increase in demand for electricity, (2) economic and technical viability of more diverse sources of energy generation, (3) the growth of distributed energy resources (DERs) and (4) states’ clean energy or decarbonization policy goals or requirements. According to 2023 filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the cumulative forecast of annual electricity load growth over the next five years has increased from 2.6% to 4.7% , with some experts cautioning that these forecasts may be underestimating actual load growth. This transformation, coupled with aging energy infrastructure; an increase in physical, natural, and cyber threats to the grid; and other constraints, has driven the need for grid modernization. Much of the energy infrastructure across the United States is aging and in need of maintenance. For example, 70 percent of transmission infrastructure is over 25 years old. In some cases, grid components are far past their 50-year life expectancies. In addition, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather storms continue to stress the energy system. There have been significant investments made by utilities, the federal government, and state, local, territorial and tribal governments to improve the reliability and resilience of the electrical grid. However, there is still work to be done to prepare the current electrical grid to meet the energy needs of the future. To modernize the electrical grids, policymakers, regulators and utilities will need to engage in thoughtful assessments and planning processes to evaluate what policy interventions, technology deployments and infrastructure buildouts are necessary to address the specific needs of their states, territories or jurisdictions. Modernizing electrical grids can include robust buildouts of energy infrastructure, such as building new or replacing and retrofitting existing transmission lines and distribution systems. Building new lines and expanding existing transmission infrastructure can increase grid capacity, power system reliability and energy affordability, but embarking on large-scale projects can be difficult, costly and take many years to implement. Investments in grid modernization technologies can improve affordability, resilience and reliability through increasing line capacity, managing demand and load, and allowing for microgrid systems to operate during grid failures. Often with lower investment costs, the benefits of technology deployments can be realized on a much shorter timescale and complement larger scale investments. A 2021 study published by the Brattle Group and WATT Coalition found that the implementation of grid-enhancing technologies could lead to $5 billion in yearly energy production cost savings, double the amount of renewable energy sources added to the grid without large-scale transmission expansions, and reduce carbon emissions by 90 million tons. Similarly, a 2023 study published by the Rocky Mountain Institute found that the deployment of grid-enhancing technologies in the PJM footprint, a regional transmission operator serving thirteen states and the District of Columbia, could yield approximately $1 billion annually in production cost savings across the region by enabling the interconnection of 6.6 gigawatts of new, low-cost renewable energy generation on the grid. Careful planning, stakeholder engagement and technical analysis is ultimately needed to optimize technology investment. An understanding of the range of technologies currently available can help Governors determine how best to initiate those processes in their states and territories. As generation facilities and the grid continue to age, threats to the grid become more prevalent, and increased demand exacerbates transmission carrying capacities. Maintaining the reliability of energy systems is becoming a greater challenge for states and territories. A resilient grid results in fewer outages, faster service restoration after an emergency, and more efficient load management. Strategic planning and assessment of electricity needs, including advanced grid technologies and other resilience strategies , can inform which technologies and investments will best address state policy goals. Thoughtful investments in decentralized energy resources and microgrids have the potential to remove strain from existing grids and allow reprioritization of other transmission and distribution needs, for example. In recent years, more frequent and severe extreme weather, rising manufacturing and data center energy demand, economic growth and transportation and building electrification have had a significant impact on electricity needs. With demand projected to increase in the future, the deployment of modern technologies can help the grid become more efficient and effectively meet demand by: (1) delivering power to end-use customers more efficiently, (2) managing demand more effectively with lower-cost supply, (3) collecting and utilizing customer data to facilitate reductions in energy consumption during high-demand, high-cost periods, and (4) requiring less investment in grid operations and maintenance. States and territories continue to look for ways to reduce the emissions and environmental impact of electricity generation by improving efficiency, reducing consumption and utilizing cleaner forms of energy generation. Many Governors have adopted broad emission reduction goals for the coming decades. As of November 2024, twenty-three states and the District of Columbia had adopted some form of decarbonization target, many of which were initiated by executive action or signed into law by Governors. Core to these solutions is the deployment of low-carbon, carbon-free and carbon neutral generation sources, including wind, solar and nuclear energy among others. Often, the lowest-cost renewable resources may not be located in close proximity to power demand and load centers, thus added transmission capacity is needed. A modernized power grid can more efficiently transmit power to where it is needed, increasing power line carrying capacity and facilitating power-sector emissions reductions. The passage of the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) created many federal incentives for grid modernization, including technology deployment. By taking advantage of these opportunities, Governors can build their state’s economy and create jobs that support grid modernization. Similarly, private industry within the energy sector is also utilizing state and federal incentives to produce innovative technologies to meet the demands for grid modernization. This has led to the commercial deployment of cost-effective and advanced grid technologies. Grid modernization supports economic development through direct job creation and by enabling the new power generation needed to support economic activity in related sectors, such as manufacturing. Additionally, ensuring reliable and affordable electricity is available to meet the electricity needs of facilities that bring economic opportunities, such as large manufacturing sites and data centers, can be facilitated through grid technology deployment. Increasingly, consumer demand is driving the incorporation of distributed energy resources (DERs), behind-the-meter resources such as rooftop solar, residential energy storage systems and electric vehicles into the fabric of U.S. electric systems and communities across the country. DER deployment can contribute to Governors’ efficiency, affordability and emissions-reductions goals. Grids are evolving to improve integration and utilization of DERs; enable intelligent, flexible, efficient and secure distribution systems; and automate grid balancing across significantly more electricity resources, both supply and demand. Grid modernizing technologies can help integrate DERs into the broader electrical grid and use the growing pool of DERs for grid services that strengthen the broader system. Advanced technologies are being integrated into electricity grids to supply energy closer to loads, maximize energy delivery capacity, and increase the effectiveness, reliability and efficiency of the energy system. These technologies can also facilitate the efficient integration of higher levels of DERs, including distributed generation (e.g., rooftop solar, fuel-based generators); storage (e.g., EV batteries, power walls); demand response; flexible demand (e.g., EV chargers, heat pumps); and more. This paper focuses on common, commercially ready technologies that modernize electric grids and identifies steps Governors can take to ensure the effective deployment of these technologies to maximize the grid. This list is by no means exhaustive, and this paper does not seek to encourage the adoption of any specific technology or endorse specific policies. The mix of technologies and policies will be determined by the needs of the grid, policy context in the state, and other factors. In 2024, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued a final rule FERC Order 1920 , updated in November 2024 under Order 1920-A , which makes significant changes to transmission planning and cost allocation. In addition to increasing the role of states in transmission planning and cost allocation, Order 1920 includes a requirement for transmission providers to consider alternative transmission technologies, including dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow controllers, and advanced conductors. In long-term and regional transmission plans, transmission owners are required to consider deployment of these technologies. It is important to recognize that these technologies should be considered holistically and deployed strategically. By making informed, deliberate decisions, policymakers, utilities and regional grid operators can leverage the right combination of technologies to meet state policy goals. Before deploying grid modernization technologies, it is important to assess the current state of grid infrastructure and how the technologies being considered can be deployed into the existing electricity system. Grid technologies will advance the reliability, affordability, and emissions-reductions goals of grid modernization only if they are able to work effectively within the energy system. To achieve this, states can consider a holistic approach to energy system planning. States and territories can holistically model the needs of the grid and impacts of these technologies through integrated transmission and distribution system planning . This process aligns the state energy planning process with the planning processes of utilities and other energy stakeholders and includes customers as a resource alongside grid resources. In addition, as regional and national energy interdependencies continue to grow, Governors can take a leading role in initiating or improving multi-state and regional planning paradigms to address grid modernization, transmission expansion and energy resilience. Similarly, high-tech innovations can often be paired with more traditional, low-tech and low-cost solutions to achieve optimal results, such as utility resilience programs that pair distribution automation with system hardening and vegetation management to improve reliability or grid-enhancing technology deployment considered alongside transmission expansion. Regardless of the approach, Governors can make key decisions that will affect how technologies are deployed. The decision to pursue new technologies to modernize electricity grids should evaluate the trade-offs of different approaches. Grid modernization has many benefits, but the deployment of these technologies can also bring costs and risks, including potential financial impacts on ratepayers (which may be balanced against longer term cost savings), cybersecurity vulnerabilities and concerns of technological development outpacing deployment. Careful study and informed decision making on the part of policymakers and the private sector is necessary to maximize benefits, mitigate risks and manage costs associated with grid modernization. There are many actions Governors can take to encourage or require the deployment of grid modernization technologies. These actions can be broken down into four categories: 1) Setting and pursuing energy policy and grid modernization goals; 2) Convening stakeholders to study and consider grid technologies; 3) Participating in regional or multistate grid modernization efforts; and 4) Working with and providing necessary resources to utility regulators. These goals can establish a Governor’s broad energy policy vision and instigate policy actions that will lead to grid modernization. For instance, Governors can: As the leaders of their state or territory, Governors have a unique opportunity to collaborate with their peers to forge interstate and regional partnerships. Electrical grids span borders and interconnects the nation. Working across state lines allows for coordination in planning and can lead to benefits for all states involved. For instance, Governors can collaborate on: NGA will be releasing a forthcoming publication that includes a detailed discussion on the history of utility regulatory models and the role Governors can play in shaping the future of utility regulation. U.S. electrical grids are critical infrastructure that keep the country moving forward. As grids age and are placed under increased stress from growing electricity demand, a new mix of generation sources, increasingly frequent extreme weather events, and an increase in physical and cyber threats, the country faces the challenge of grid modernization to meet the energy needs of the future while delivering new value to residents. There is no single way to modernize and improve electrical grids. Governors can consider the use of grid modernization technologies as one means of doing so. The deployment of grid modernization technologies provides various benefits to the grid and supports the achievement of efficiency, reliability, affordability and decarbonization goals. It is important to recognize the benefits, costs, risks and other factors associated with the adoption of grid technologies and how their deployment would impact the broader energy system and energy consumers. Governors can guide the consideration of tradeoffs in adopting grid modernization technologies by setting clear policy goals, encouraging collaboration, and ensuring decision-makers explore new technologies and policies to meet grid modernization needs. This paper was authored by Fiona Forrester, Policy Analyst, National Governors Association, with guidance from Dan Lauf, Program Director, Energy, National Governors Association. For more information, please email fforrester@nga.org and dlauf@nga.org . NGA would like to thank the many partners who reviewed drafts of this paper and provided helpful input on the content:

Grid modernization supports economic development through direct job creation and by enabling the new power generation needed to support economic activity in related sectors, such as manufacturing. Additionally, ensuring reliable and affordable electricity is available to meet the electricity needs of facilities that bring economic opportunities, such as large manufacturing sites and data centers, can be facilitated through grid technology deployment.

Increasingly, consumer demand is driving the incorporation of distributed energy resources (DERs), behind-the-meter resources such as rooftop solar, residential energy storage systems and electric vehicles into the fabric of U.S. electric systems and communities across the country. DER deployment can contribute to Governors’ efficiency, affordability and emissions-reductions goals. Grids are evolving to improve integration and utilization of DERs; enable intelligent, flexible, efficient and secure distribution systems; and automate grid balancing across significantly more electricity resources, both supply and demand. Grid modernizing technologies can help integrate DERs into the broader electrical grid and use the growing pool of DERs for grid services that strengthen the broader system.

Advanced technologies are being integrated into electricity grids to supply energy closer to loads, maximize energy delivery capacity, and increase the effectiveness, reliability and efficiency of the energy system. These technologies can also facilitate the efficient integration of higher levels of DERs, including distributed generation (e.g., rooftop solar, fuel-based generators); storage (e.g., EV batteries, power walls); demand response; flexible demand (e.g., EV chargers, heat pumps); and more.

This paper focuses on common, commercially ready technologies that modernize electric grids and identifies steps Governors can take to ensure the effective deployment of these technologies to maximize the grid. This list is by no means exhaustive, and this paper does not seek to encourage the adoption of any specific technology or endorse specific policies. The mix of technologies and policies will be determined by the needs of the grid, policy context in the state, and other factors.

In 2024, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued a final rule FERC Order 1920 , updated in November 2024 under Order 1920-A , which makes significant changes to transmission planning and cost allocation. In addition to increasing the role of states in transmission planning and cost allocation, Order 1920 includes a requirement for transmission providers to consider alternative transmission technologies, including dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow controllers, and advanced conductors. In long-term and regional transmission plans, transmission owners are required to consider deployment of these technologies.

It is important to recognize that these technologies should be considered holistically and deployed strategically. By making informed, deliberate decisions, policymakers, utilities and regional grid operators can leverage the right combination of technologies to meet state policy goals. Before deploying grid modernization technologies, it is important to assess the current state of grid infrastructure and how the technologies being considered can be deployed into the existing electricity system. Grid technologies will advance the reliability, affordability, and emissions-reductions goals of grid modernization only if they are able to work effectively within the energy system. To achieve this, states can consider a holistic approach to energy system planning.

States and territories can holistically model the needs of the grid and impacts of these technologies through integrated transmission and distribution system planning . This process aligns the state energy planning process with the planning processes of utilities and other energy stakeholders and includes customers as a resource alongside grid resources. In addition, as regional and national energy interdependencies continue to grow, Governors can take a leading role in initiating or improving multi-state and regional planning paradigms to address grid modernization, transmission expansion and energy resilience.

Similarly, high-tech innovations can often be paired with more traditional, low-tech and low-cost solutions to achieve optimal results, such as utility resilience programs that pair distribution automation with system hardening and vegetation management to improve reliability or grid-enhancing technology deployment considered alongside transmission expansion. Regardless of the approach, Governors can make key decisions that will affect how technologies are deployed.

The decision to pursue new technologies to modernize electricity grids should evaluate the trade-offs of different approaches. Grid modernization has many benefits, but the deployment of these technologies can also bring costs and risks, including potential financial impacts on ratepayers (which may be balanced against longer term cost savings), cybersecurity vulnerabilities and concerns of technological development outpacing deployment. Careful study and informed decision making on the part of policymakers and the private sector is necessary to maximize benefits, mitigate risks and manage costs associated with grid modernization. There are many actions Governors can take to encourage or require the deployment of grid modernization technologies. These actions can be broken down into four categories: 1) Setting and pursuing energy policy and grid modernization goals; 2) Convening stakeholders to study and consider grid technologies; 3) Participating in regional or multistate grid modernization efforts; and 4) Working with and providing necessary resources to utility regulators.
These goals can establish a Governor’s broad energy policy vision and instigate policy actions that will lead to grid modernization. For instance, Governors can:

As the leaders of their state or territory, Governors have a unique opportunity to collaborate with their peers to forge interstate and regional partnerships. Electrical grids span borders and interconnects the nation. Working across state lines allows for coordination in planning and can lead to benefits for all states involved. For instance, Governors can collaborate on:

NGA will be releasing a forthcoming publication that includes a detailed discussion on the history of utility regulatory models and the role Governors can play in shaping the future of utility regulation.

U.S. electrical grids are critical infrastructure that keep the country moving forward. As grids age and are placed under increased stress from growing electricity demand, a new mix of generation sources, increasingly frequent extreme weather events, and an increase in physical and cyber threats, the country faces the challenge of grid modernization to meet the energy needs of the future while delivering new value to residents. There is no single way to modernize and improve electrical grids. Governors can consider the use of grid modernization technologies as one means of doing so.

The deployment of grid modernization technologies provides various benefits to the grid and supports the achievement of efficiency, reliability, affordability and decarbonization goals. It is important to recognize the benefits, costs, risks and other factors associated with the adoption of grid technologies and how their deployment would impact the broader energy system and energy consumers. Governors can guide the consideration of tradeoffs in adopting grid modernization technologies by setting clear policy goals, encouraging collaboration, and ensuring decision-makers explore new technologies and policies to meet grid modernization needs.

extraction.body: Pictured: Jonathan McGinnis, project manager for Heimdall Power; Ann Charlotte Valheim, chief deployment officer, Heimdall Power; and Tim Sansing, senior engineer, Entergy. What if more electricity could safely move across some existing transmission lines without the immediate need for building new ones? That’s the opportunity behind advanced transmission technology being deployed across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi — and one of the most innovative parts of the project arrives by drone. Through a $13.7 million U.S. Department of Energy award , this project will deploy dynamic line rating technology and other grid improvements across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines. The goal is to increase power capacity, reduce congestion and strengthen the grid as communities across our region continue to grow. DLR has been around for decades, but advances in technology have made it more practical and scalable. Katie Jereza, assistant secretary for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Electricity, joined Entergy leaders in Mississippi this week for a project tour and press conference . “DLR is not a new concept, but the installation method and how we go about deploying this is the new piece of it that finally makes it something that people can see the benefit and actually get behind,” said Tim Sansing, senior engineer for technology development and analytics. At the center of the effort are small sensors attached directly to transmission lines that provide live information about conditions such as temperature, wind speed, solar radiation, conductor temperature and line sag. “DLR gives us real-time insight into how much electricity a line can safely carry under actual weather conditions, helping us move more energy across the grid using existing infrastructure,” Sansing said. One way to further understand DLR is to compare it to a highway. Drivers follow a posted speed limit because it provides a safe operating standard, but conditions such as weather can change from one day to the next. Similarly, DLR provides additional information about real-time conditions on a transmission line, giving operators greater visibility into how much capacity may be available at a given time while maintaining safety and reliability. One of the most innovative aspects of the project is the way sensors are installed. Instead of relying on a bucket truck, an outage or extensive manual work, an autonomous drone carries each sensor to the transmission line. Using LiDAR technology, the drone identifies the conductor and completes the installation in less than two minutes. That approach is especially valuable when deploying more than 600 sensors across 1,100-plus miles of transmission lines, including in rural and difficult-to-access areas. The technology also provides greater visibility into portions of the transmission system that historically has had less real-time information available. As this technology develops, the sensors could support additional capabilities, including wildfire detection and connections to other devices such as cameras. While the drone may be the most visible part of the project, the larger opportunity is making better use of existing infrastructure as electricity demand grows across our region, including new industrial development, manufacturing and data centers. Increasing capacity on existing lines could help defer some future transmission investments, which can take years to plan and build, while providing operators with more information to manage changing conditions across the system. “We’re doing everything we can to keep the cost down for customers and be able to get the most that we can out of what we have today, rather than having to rely on new builds,” Sansing said. The project also includes targeted substations and terminal upgrades designed to help maximize the benefits of the technology where existing equipment could otherwise limit capacity. Ultimately, the goal is to use innovation to make better use of infrastructure already in place, strengthen the grid and support the communities and industries that depend on reliable electricity. Sometimes, that innovation takes flight.
