extraction.body: This paper is part of a series published by the National Governors Association (NGA) to identify actions Governors can take to guide their states and territories through intentional and effective power sector transformations. This paper provides a deeper dive into actions Governors can take to modernize the grid through the deployment of grid technologies. Electric power grids in the United States are in a period of rapid transformation, driven by a confluence of factors such as an increase in electricity demand, retirement of certain baseload power generation, an increase in distributed generation, lengthy interconnection queues and new “grid-edge” technologies being brought online. Layered into this evolution are new state and national decarbonization objectives, heightened awareness of the magnitude and frequency of threats that could compromise reliable power delivery, and unprecedented federal investment through legislation like the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). With these transformative trends in process, Governors are eager to support deployment of technology solutions to facilitate their policy objectives and meet increased loads – and doing so while maintaining or even improving grid reliability, resilience and affordability. This paper is part of a series published by the National Governors Association (NGA) to identify actions Governors can take to guide their states and territories through intentional and effective power sector transformations. While other papers explore regulatory structures, regional markets and power transmission, this paper provides a deeper dive into actions Governors can take to modernize the grid through the deployment of grid technologies. While careful planning, stakeholder engagement and robust technical analysis is needed to optimize technology investment, an understanding of the range of technologies currently available can help Governors determine how best to initiate or improve those processes in their states and territories. Often a combination of technologies will best allow states and grid operators to meet their objectives. While by no means exhaustive, this paper will focus on several of the grid modernizing technologies that are commercially available and being deployed: Underpinning modernization of the electric grid are regulatory structures and robust planning processes that work to meet specific objectives, such as resilience, reliability, affordability or decarbonization. Strengthening these structures and approaching grid modernization from a comprehensive planning perspective will create an environment for sustained innovation within the electrical sector. Governors’ strategies to guide the deployment of grid modernizing technologies addressed in this paper include: The electrical grid of the United States supports all aspects of the economy, as well as the safety of all Americans. From powering homes, schools and businesses to critical infrastructure and industries, the safe, reliable and affordable flow of electricity is essential to modern life. The electric grids have evolved from a loosely connected set of systems to a vast network of interconnected infrastructure serving hundreds of millions of customers. The electrical grid is undergoing a robust transformation, driven by (1) an increase in demand for electricity, (2) economic and technical viability of more diverse sources of energy generation, (3) the growth of distributed energy resources (DERs) and (4) states’ clean energy or decarbonization policy goals or requirements. According to 2023 filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the cumulative forecast of annual electricity load growth over the next five years has increased from 2.6% to 4.7% , with some experts cautioning that these forecasts may be underestimating actual load growth. This transformation, coupled with aging energy infrastructure; an increase in physical, natural, and cyber threats to the grid; and other constraints, has driven the need for grid modernization. Much of the energy infrastructure across the United States is aging and in need of maintenance. For example, 70 percent of transmission infrastructure is over 25 years old. In some cases, grid components are far past their 50-year life expectancies. In addition, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather storms continue to stress the energy system. There have been significant investments made by utilities, the federal government, and state, local, territorial and tribal governments to improve the reliability and resilience of the electrical grid. However, there is still work to be done to prepare the current electrical grid to meet the energy needs of the future. To modernize the electrical grids, policymakers, regulators and utilities will need to engage in thoughtful assessments and planning processes to evaluate what policy interventions, technology deployments and infrastructure buildouts are necessary to address the specific needs of their states, territories or jurisdictions. Modernizing electrical grids can include robust buildouts of energy infrastructure, such as building new or replacing and retrofitting existing transmission lines and distribution systems. Building new lines and expanding existing transmission infrastructure can increase grid capacity, power system reliability and energy affordability, but embarking on large-scale projects can be difficult, costly and take many years to implement. Investments in grid modernization technologies can improve affordability, resilience and reliability through increasing line capacity, managing demand and load, and allowing for microgrid systems to operate during grid failures. Often with lower investment costs, the benefits of technology deployments can be realized on a much shorter timescale and complement larger scale investments. A 2021 study published by the Brattle Group and WATT Coalition found that the implementation of grid-enhancing technologies could lead to $5 billion in yearly energy production cost savings, double the amount of renewable energy sources added to the grid without large-scale transmission expansions, and reduce carbon emissions by 90 million tons. Similarly, a 2023 study published by the Rocky Mountain Institute found that the deployment of grid-enhancing technologies in the PJM footprint, a regional transmission operator serving thirteen states and the District of Columbia, could yield approximately $1 billion annually in production cost savings across the region by enabling the interconnection of 6.6 gigawatts of new, low-cost renewable energy generation on the grid. Careful planning, stakeholder engagement and technical analysis is ultimately needed to optimize technology investment. An understanding of the range of technologies currently available can help Governors determine how best to initiate those processes in their states and territories. As generation facilities and the grid continue to age, threats to the grid become more prevalent, and increased demand exacerbates transmission carrying capacities. Maintaining the reliability of energy systems is becoming a greater challenge for states and territories. A resilient grid results in fewer outages, faster service restoration after an emergency, and more efficient load management. Strategic planning and assessment of electricity needs, including advanced grid technologies and other resilience strategies , can inform which technologies and investments will best address state policy goals. Thoughtful investments in decentralized energy resources and microgrids have the potential to remove strain from existing grids and allow reprioritization of other transmission and distribution needs, for example. In recent years, more frequent and severe extreme weather, rising manufacturing and data center energy demand, economic growth and transportation and building electrification have had a significant impact on electricity needs. With demand projected to increase in the future, the deployment of modern technologies can help the grid become more efficient and effectively meet demand by: (1) delivering power to end-use customers more efficiently, (2) managing demand more effectively with lower-cost supply, (3) collecting and utilizing customer data to facilitate reductions in energy consumption during high-demand, high-cost periods, and (4) requiring less investment in grid operations and maintenance. States and territories continue to look for ways to reduce the emissions and environmental impact of electricity generation by improving efficiency, reducing consumption and utilizing cleaner forms of energy generation. Many Governors have adopted broad emission reduction goals for the coming decades. As of November 2024, twenty-three states and the District of Columbia had adopted some form of decarbonization target, many of which were initiated by executive action or signed into law by Governors. Core to these solutions is the deployment of low-carbon, carbon-free and carbon neutral generation sources, including wind, solar and nuclear energy among others. Often, the lowest-cost renewable resources may not be located in close proximity to power demand and load centers, thus added transmission capacity is needed. A modernized power grid can more efficiently transmit power to where it is needed, increasing power line carrying capacity and facilitating power-sector emissions reductions. The passage of the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) created many federal incentives for grid modernization, including technology deployment. By taking advantage of these opportunities, Governors can build their state’s economy and create jobs that support grid modernization. Similarly, private industry within the energy sector is also utilizing state and federal incentives to produce innovative technologies to meet the demands for grid modernization. This has led to the commercial deployment of cost-effective and advanced grid technologies. Grid modernization supports economic development through direct job creation and by enabling the new power generation needed to support economic activity in related sectors, such as manufacturing. Additionally, ensuring reliable and affordable electricity is available to meet the electricity needs of facilities that bring economic opportunities, such as large manufacturing sites and data centers, can be facilitated through grid technology deployment. Increasingly, consumer demand is driving the incorporation of distributed energy resources (DERs), behind-the-meter resources such as rooftop solar, residential energy storage systems and electric vehicles into the fabric of U.S. electric systems and communities across the country. DER deployment can contribute to Governors’ efficiency, affordability and emissions-reductions goals. Grids are evolving to improve integration and utilization of DERs; enable intelligent, flexible, efficient and secure distribution systems; and automate grid balancing across significantly more electricity resources, both supply and demand. Grid modernizing technologies can help integrate DERs into the broader electrical grid and use the growing pool of DERs for grid services that strengthen the broader system. Advanced technologies are being integrated into electricity grids to supply energy closer to loads, maximize energy delivery capacity, and increase the effectiveness, reliability and efficiency of the energy system. These technologies can also facilitate the efficient integration of higher levels of DERs, including distributed generation (e.g., rooftop solar, fuel-based generators); storage (e.g., EV batteries, power walls); demand response; flexible demand (e.g., EV chargers, heat pumps); and more. This paper focuses on common, commercially ready technologies that modernize electric grids and identifies steps Governors can take to ensure the effective deployment of these technologies to maximize the grid. This list is by no means exhaustive, and this paper does not seek to encourage the adoption of any specific technology or endorse specific policies. The mix of technologies and policies will be determined by the needs of the grid, policy context in the state, and other factors. In 2024, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued a final rule FERC Order 1920 , updated in November 2024 under Order 1920-A , which makes significant changes to transmission planning and cost allocation. In addition to increasing the role of states in transmission planning and cost allocation, Order 1920 includes a requirement for transmission providers to consider alternative transmission technologies, including dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow controllers, and advanced conductors. In long-term and regional transmission plans, transmission owners are required to consider deployment of these technologies. It is important to recognize that these technologies should be considered holistically and deployed strategically. By making informed, deliberate decisions, policymakers, utilities and regional grid operators can leverage the right combination of technologies to meet state policy goals. Before deploying grid modernization technologies, it is important to assess the current state of grid infrastructure and how the technologies being considered can be deployed into the existing electricity system. Grid technologies will advance the reliability, affordability, and emissions-reductions goals of grid modernization only if they are able to work effectively within the energy system. To achieve this, states can consider a holistic approach to energy system planning. States and territories can holistically model the needs of the grid and impacts of these technologies through integrated transmission and distribution system planning . This process aligns the state energy planning process with the planning processes of utilities and other energy stakeholders and includes customers as a resource alongside grid resources. In addition, as regional and national energy interdependencies continue to grow, Governors can take a leading role in initiating or improving multi-state and regional planning paradigms to address grid modernization, transmission expansion and energy resilience. Similarly, high-tech innovations can often be paired with more traditional, low-tech and low-cost solutions to achieve optimal results, such as utility resilience programs that pair distribution automation with system hardening and vegetation management to improve reliability or grid-enhancing technology deployment considered alongside transmission expansion. Regardless of the approach, Governors can make key decisions that will affect how technologies are deployed. The decision to pursue new technologies to modernize electricity grids should evaluate the trade-offs of different approaches. Grid modernization has many benefits, but the deployment of these technologies can also bring costs and risks, including potential financial impacts on ratepayers (which may be balanced against longer term cost savings), cybersecurity vulnerabilities and concerns of technological development outpacing deployment. Careful study and informed decision making on the part of policymakers and the private sector is necessary to maximize benefits, mitigate risks and manage costs associated with grid modernization. There are many actions Governors can take to encourage or require the deployment of grid modernization technologies. These actions can be broken down into four categories: 1) Setting and pursuing energy policy and grid modernization goals; 2) Convening stakeholders to study and consider grid technologies; 3) Participating in regional or multistate grid modernization efforts; and 4) Working with and providing necessary resources to utility regulators. These goals can establish a Governor’s broad energy policy vision and instigate policy actions that will lead to grid modernization. For instance, Governors can: As the leaders of their state or territory, Governors have a unique opportunity to collaborate with their peers to forge interstate and regional partnerships. Electrical grids span borders and interconnects the nation. Working across state lines allows for coordination in planning and can lead to benefits for all states involved. U.S. electrical grids are critical infrastructure that keep the country moving forward. As grids age and are placed under increased stress from growing electricity demand, a new mix of generation sources, increasingly frequent extreme weather events, and an increase in physical and cyber threats, the country faces the challenge of grid modernization to meet the energy needs of the future while delivering new value to residents. There is no single way to modernize and improve electrical grids. Governors can consider the use of grid modernization technologies as one means of doing so. The deployment of grid modernization technologies provides various benefits to the grid and supports the achievement of efficiency, reliability, affordability and decarbonization goals. It is important to recognize the benefits, costs, risks and other factors associated with the adoption of grid technologies and how their deployment would impact the broader energy system and energy consumers. Governors can guide the consideration of tradeoffs in adopting grid modernization technologies by setting clear policy goals, encouraging collaboration, and ensuring decision-makers explore new technologies and policies to meet grid modernization needs. Strengthening these structures and approaching grid modernization from a comprehensive planning perspective will create an environment for sustained innovation within the electrical sector.

In addition to increasing the role of states in transmission planning and cost allocation, Order 1920 includes a requirement for transmission providers to consider alternative transmission technologies, including dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow controllers, and advanced conductors.

Advanced technologies are being integrated into electricity grids to supply energy closer to loads, maximize energy delivery capacity, and increase the effectiveness, reliability and efficiency of the energy system.

extraction.body: Pictured: Jonathan McGinnis, project manager for Heimdall Power; Ann Charlotte Valheim, chief deployment officer, Heimdall Power; and Tim Sansing, senior engineer, Entergy. What if more electricity could safely move across some existing transmission lines without the immediate need for building new ones? That’s the opportunity behind advanced transmission technology being deployed across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi — and one of the most innovative parts of the project arrives by drone. Through a $13.7 million U.S. Department of Energy award , this project will deploy dynamic line rating technology and other grid improvements across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines. The goal is to increase power capacity, reduce congestion and strengthen the grid as communities across our region continue to grow. DLR has been around for decades, but advances in technology have made it more practical and scalable. Katie Jereza, assistant secretary for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Electricity, joined Entergy leaders in Mississippi this week for a project tour and press conference . “DLR is not a new concept, but the installation method and how we go about deploying this is the new piece of it that finally makes it something that people can see the benefit and actually get behind,” said Tim Sansing, senior engineer for technology development and analytics. At the center of the effort are small sensors attached directly to transmission lines that provide live information about conditions such as temperature, wind speed, solar radiation, conductor temperature and line sag. “DLR gives us real-time insight into how much electricity a line can safely carry under actual weather conditions, helping us move more energy across the grid using existing infrastructure,” Sansing said. One way to further understand DLR is to compare it to a highway. Drivers follow a posted speed limit because it provides a safe operating standard, but conditions such as weather can change from one day to the next. Similarly, DLR provides additional information about real-time conditions on a transmission line, giving operators greater visibility into how much capacity may be available at a given time while maintaining safety and reliability. One of the most innovative aspects of the project is the way sensors are installed. Instead of relying on a bucket truck, an outage or extensive manual work, an autonomous drone carries each sensor to the transmission line. Using LiDAR technology, the drone identifies the conductor and completes the installation in less than two minutes. That approach is especially valuable when deploying more than 600 sensors across 1,100-plus miles of transmission lines, including in rural and difficult-to-access areas. The technology also provides greater visibility into portions of the transmission system that historically has had less real-time information available. As this technology develops, the sensors could support additional capabilities, including wildfire detection and connections to other devices such as cameras. While the drone may be the most visible part of the project, the larger opportunity is making better use of existing infrastructure as electricity demand grows across our region, including new industrial development, manufacturing and data centers. Increasing capacity on existing lines could help defer some future transmission investments, which can take years to plan and build, while providing operators with more information to manage changing conditions across the system. “We’re doing everything we can to keep the cost down for customers and be able to get the most that we can out of what we have today, rather than having to rely on new builds,” Sansing said. The project also includes targeted substations and terminal upgrades designed to help maximize the benefits of the technology where existing equipment could otherwise limit capacity. Ultimately, the goal is to use innovation to make better use of infrastructure already in place, strengthen the grid and support the communities and industries that depend on reliable electricity. Sometimes, that innovation takes flight. Despite quite a few predictions to the contrary, a Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) "supercycle" probably isn't coming anytime soon, and past supercycle calls have a poor record. That hasn't dented the conviction of James Thorne, chief market strategist at Canadian wealth manager Wellington-Altus Private Wealth, who said he expects a run "for the ages" on Oct. 15 in an interview with Bitcoin Magazine . Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Thorne's argument is that Bitcoin's four-year cycle, a theory that describes its booms and busts as being anchored by its halvings, is no longer relevant. Citing his experience with trading during the commodities supercycle starting in the early 2000s, he claims that the crypto market structure has changed such that this time will be different. One cause of those changes is the Genius Act, which is the U.S. law regulating stablecoins, and also an increasing trend toward tokenization of assets, which means recording the ownership of assets like Treasury bonds on a blockchain. While the stablecoin regulations could pave the way for more usable capital to live on blockchain rails, asset tokenization could bring more capital tied up in assets from the traditional financial system into crypto as well. Another element supporting Thorne's argument is that regulators approved spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on Jan. 10, 2024, so Wall Street had easy access to the coin throughout the last market cycle. As of Oct. 20, those funds had drawn $57.8 billion in cumulative net inflows. Thorne is correct to assume that cryptoasset prices are very likely to rise over the long run as a result of these factors. But the term "supercycle" has no real fixed definition. It's a term that's hypothesized about pretty much every crypto market cycle. And it's most commonly trotted out during the early innings of a new bull market , which we might be in right now. For example, in 2021, crypto fund manager Su Zhu predicted that crypto would rise consistently without any new prolonged bear markets, only to later repudiate the thesis in May 2022. The most recent market cycle, centered around the 2024 halving, also saw more than its fair share of supercycle predictions that didn't play out, due in part to the coin breaching its former all-time high in advance of the halving for the first time. Investors shouldn't buy into the supercycle claims. There will likely always be bear markets for Bitcoin, just as there are for other assets with institutional support. And even if that wasn't true, the implied best course of action is the same. Accumulate Bitcoin gradually in small amounts over time. Don't buy so much that you compromise your portfolio's diversification, and don't buy more than you can afford to lose. If there's a bear market, keep buying the same amount (or a hair more) as when there's a bull market underway, and hold for at least five years. extraction.body: Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater Associates, has softened his stance on Bitcoin ( BTC -0.50% ) over the years. In 2017, he called it a bubble and said it's "not an effective storehold of wealth." But now, in an article he published on Aug. 21, he recommended that investors hold "a bit of Bitcoin," as he believes most economies face debt and deficit problems. He considers non-government-produced money like Bitcoin to be one way to navigate this risk, and he expects it will do relatively well. As far as how much "a bit" is, Dalio has previously said that allocating up to 2% of your portfolio to Bitcoin is reasonable. Even though I own Bitcoin, I disagree with Dalio's recommendation that risk mitigation is a reason to hold the cryptocurrency. Bridgewater Associates Founder Ray Dalio. Image source: Getty Images. Dalio recommended Bitcoin in response to a question about how investors should navigate the risk of a debt crisis and position their portfolios going forward. In fairness, he mentions gold first, with a suggested allocation of 10%-15% to reduce risk. But despite Bitcoin sometimes being called digital gold, it doesn't provide the same level of protection. Bitcoin typically moves in the same direction as stocks. The S&P 500 and Bitcoin moved in the same direction in eight out of 10 years from 2016 through 2025, according to recent research by The Motley Fool . That includes 2022's bear market, when Bitcoin lost about three times as much as the S&P 500. If a debt crisis sends the stock market into a tailspin, Bitcoin could react similarly or even worse. It's a different story when comparing gold versus stocks . The two tend to move in opposite directions, and in 2022, gold managed to hold its value, growing by a modest 0.3%. If you're worried about a bear market, gold is likely to help reduce losses in your portfolio more than Bitcoin would. Bitcoin can be a good addition to your portfolio if you want exposure to digital assets and you have a high risk tolerance. While extremely volatile, it has had periods where it outperformed the market by a wide margin, including 2024 and 2025. If you're interested in Bitcoin, you can invest in the cryptocurrency itself or Bitcoin ETFs , and Dalio's guideline of up to 2% Bitcoin allocation is reasonable. Experienced crypto investors may want to go a little higher and possibly branch out to other cryptocurrencies, as well, but limiting your exposure is smart with such volatile assets. However, you can also put together a well-rounded portfolio with just stocks and bonds. And if it's risk reduction you're after, Bitcoin isn't the best choice. Lyle Daly has positions in Bitcoin. extraction.body: Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater Associates, has softened his stance on Bitcoin ( BTC -0.50% ) over the years. In 2017, he called it a bubble and said it's "not an effective storehold of wealth." But now, in an article he published on Aug. 21, he recommended that investors hold "a bit of Bitcoin," as he believes most economies face debt and deficit problems. He considers non-government-produced money like Bitcoin to be one way to navigate this risk, and he expects it will do relatively well. As far as how much "a bit" is, Dalio has previously said that allocating up to 2% of your portfolio to Bitcoin is reasonable. Even though I own Bitcoin, I disagree with Dalio's recommendation that risk mitigation is a reason to hold the cryptocurrency. Bridgewater Associates Founder Ray Dalio. Image source: Getty Images. Dalio recommended Bitcoin in response to a question about how investors should navigate the risk of a debt crisis and position their portfolios going forward. In fairness, he mentions gold first, with a suggested allocation of 10%-15% to reduce risk. But despite Bitcoin sometimes being called digital gold, it doesn't provide the same level of protection. Bitcoin typically moves in the same direction as stocks. The S&P 500 and Bitcoin moved in the same direction in eight out of 10 years from 2016 through 2025, according to recent research by The Motley Fool . That includes 2022's bear market, when Bitcoin lost about three times as much as the S&P 500. If a debt crisis sends the stock market into a tailspin, Bitcoin could react similarly or even worse. It's a different story when comparing gold versus stocks . The two tend to move in opposite directions, and in 2022, gold managed to hold its value, growing by a modest 0.3%. If you're worried about a bear market, gold is likely to help reduce losses in your portfolio more than Bitcoin would. Bitcoin can be a good addition to your portfolio if you want exposure to digital assets and you have a high risk tolerance. While extremely volatile, it has had periods where it outperformed the market by a wide margin, including 2024 and 2025. If you're interested in Bitcoin, you can invest in the cryptocurrency itself or Bitcoin ETFs , and Dalio's guideline of up to 2% Bitcoin allocation is reasonable. Experienced crypto investors may want to go a little higher and possibly branch out to other cryptocurrencies, as well, but limiting your exposure is smart with such volatile assets. However, you can also put together a well-rounded portfolio with just stocks and bonds. And if it's risk reduction you're after, Bitcoin isn't the best choice. Lyle Daly has positions in Bitcoin. The practice, helmed by Chris Dixon, has raised nearly $10 billion across five funds since launching in 2018, backing some of the sector’s biggest wins, including Coinbase. Yet for years, a16z and rival venture firms struggled to push crypto’s utility beyond financial rails, trading applications, and speculative assets. Under the new name, the team is broadening its mandate to focus on emerging technologies, be it AI, robotics, or “new kinds of networks” connecting humans and machines. Yet, the group isn’t abandoning crypto. Dixon wrote in a blog post that blockchain technology could “give new networks native economic capabilities.” Alongside Dixon, a16z Frontier’s general partners include Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet. passages: Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it.
Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control.
The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions.

Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote.
“Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S.
Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr.
Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr.
Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.”
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it.

Proposition 40 , which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state.
The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax.
According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm.
Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes.
The filing also describes how the plan would work.
Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own.
The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says.

The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class.

extraction.body: During Meta’s earnings call on Wednesday, the company revealed its board had approved a new class of nonvoting stock, called Class C common stock. The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions. This class takes effect in January. Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote. Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it. Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control. Proposition 40 , which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state. Backers say the policy could generate as much as $100 billion over five years, the bulk of which would be used to pay for the state’s healthcare needs, with the rest being used for food assistance and education. The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes. The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class. The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August. The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says. That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake. When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.” It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax. Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize. “Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes.
The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class.

The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August.

The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says.

That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.”
It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax.

Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize.

“Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.

extraction.body: OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company . TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost. Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost. “The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.” Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically. In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness. Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements. Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter. The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.” Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well. Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?” As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

extraction.body: In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss. Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee. In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare. The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France , India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee. Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern , with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.” Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.” Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied : “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?” Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways. “The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said. Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits . While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College. “Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.” In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project. Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products. If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement. In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE. Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise. The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods. Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon — widely known as the "Spy Sheikh" because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million. The company told The Wall Street Journal , which revealed the transaction in January 2026, that Trump had no involvement in the deal. But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures. The lawsuit also highlights a "scheme" by an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund chaired by Tahnoon to "inflate the value of President Trump's crypto holdings" through last year's purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty's stablecoin, USD1. The lawsuit asserts the conduct violates the U.S. Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause, which forbids federal officeholders from accepting money or other gifts from foreign officials without the consent of Congress. "This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, counsel for World Liberty Financial, said in a statement. "All we know about it is from media reports. Anyone can file a lawsuit in America, even a frivolous one." "This is yet another frivolous lawsuit that echoes the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement. passages: Elon Musk has invested approximately $1 billion in the newly formed media company Skydance, according to a new report from Semafor .
News of the investment comes a few weeks after Paramount completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros.
Semafor reports that Musk’s investment was made around the same time as equity contributions from other Skydance investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs.
The investment will provide a much needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price, the report notes.
Skydance has already committed to reducing costs by $6 billion over the next three years.
Skydance did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

sources.title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
passages: The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.
Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google.
In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it.
The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs.
You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios.
Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus.

sources.title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
passages: Today, it’s exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain “foreign surveillance chips,” the FCC claims.

The agency doesn’t say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the “surveillance chip”: it’s a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC, a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like.
On October 13th, Brendan Carr’s FCC gave itself a new power — it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security.
It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets, and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters.

It’s often sold as a package with a Sony camera sensor and sometimes even a lens already on board, according to listings we viewed on AliExpress. The FCC is calling it a foreign surveillance chip because HiVision advertises it as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC explains — and because HiVision is a subsidiary of Huawei, one of the first telecom companies the US government decided to call a national security risk. Huawei is indeed on the FCC’s Covered List, and the FCC’s new power helps it close a loophole where companies could sneak in banned companies’ products inside another company’s gadgets. It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets, and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters. As with the router ban and the Roomba ban, he question remains: is the FCC keeping people safer, or just picking winners and losers while making a show of enforcement?

sources.title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace - CNBC
passages: Etsy said Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform.
Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces.
The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns.
Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said.
"Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote.
"It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.

And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items."
Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling.
Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods.

The company has been leaning more into that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart , as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein.
Etsy said in a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform.
Etsy has also partnered with OpenAI on shopping features, including launching a ChatGPT app for product discovery.

Sellers will also be required to show an actual item made using the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, "so buyers know what to expect," Etsy said. "Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote. "It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. As part of the move, Etsy said it's barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling. Etsy told sellers it will continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform as long as merchants "play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process." "Sellers must still disclose when an item is created using AI and cannot misrepresent AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own creation," the company added. passages: While HIPAA eligible is an AWS designation, HIPAA compliant is a property of your entire environment.
HIPAA eligible means AWS has assessed the service and permits you to use it to process, store, and transmit PHI under a signed AWS BAA.
Amazon Quick eligibility serves only as a building block.
That alone doesn’t make your application and environment HIPAA compliant.

You still need to sign the BAA, classify your data, configure the controls correctly, and own the administrative and physical safeguards HIPAA requires, including workforce training, risk analysis, and breach procedures that AWS doesn’t perform for you.
An eligible service such as Amazon Quick, a signed BAA, correct configuration, governance, and your own safeguards is what produces a HIPAA-compliant deployment.
Amazon Quick being eligible means you can build a compliant workflow on it.
It doesn’t mean that turning it on makes you automatically compliant.
We close with a step-by-step implementation guide, a conclusion, and resources for deeper reading.

Amazon Quick gives regulated healthcare organizations, and the business associates who serve them, a managed AI workspace that is HIPAA-eligible across its full range of capabilities: agentic AI, knowledge retrieval, business intelligence, automation, and research.
Covered entities and business associates must both sign a business associate addendum (BAA) before PHI changes hands.
Amazon Quick agents don’t wait for instructions at every step.
They invoke tools, modify data, and interact with external systems on their own.
That changes how you approach securing your environment.
AWS published four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026, and they apply directly here.
This post, however, focuses on the capabilities of the Amazon Quick web version, which you access through your browser.

But the de-identification, the ETL, and the lake-level grants happen upstream in Glue, Glue DataBrew, and Lake Formation.
This division is the recommended pattern, and is the practical answer to augmenting Amazon Quick in a federated environment.

Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response.
An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further.
Agents might retrieve data from both unstructured and structured sources, call other systems through connectors, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf.
You can also add your own custom tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Only connectors authorized within your organization are visible.

When a chat agent can both read and act on PHI, you need sufficient governance: deterministic guardrails, a behavioral audit trail of what the agent did, and clear accountability for actions taken without a person in the loop.

→ Amazon Quick Sight dataset ( Amazon Athena ) (row-level and column-level security, run-as role)
The compliance expectations are moving as fast as the technology.
Organizations that build on deterministic, infrastructure-level controls today will likely be well positioned as regulatory expectations catch up to what agentic AI can do.
If your organization requires control of its own encryption keys, register a customer managed key as the account default before creating any Amazon Quick AI resources.

extraction.body: Protected Health Information (PHI) is any information that identifies a person and relates to their health, care, or payment for care, such as a medical note, a claim, or a member ID. When software touches PHI, it falls under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), the federal law that governs how PHI data is accessed, secured, and audited. Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response. An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further. For example, its chat agents work across both unstructured content, such as clinical notes and appeals letters, and structured data, such as claims and member records. Agents might retrieve data from both unstructured and structured sources, call other systems through connectors, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf. Connectors are pre-built integrations that let Amazon Quick securely read from and take action in your external systems, such as Slack , Microsoft Outlook , Salesforce , Atlassian Jira , and Microsoft SharePoint . You can also add your own custom tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Only connectors authorized within your organization are visible. When a chat agent can both read and act on PHI, you need sufficient governance: deterministic guardrails, a behavioral audit trail of what the agent did, and clear accountability for actions taken without a person in the loop. To support that governance, Amazon Quick exposes ACL-aware retrieval, chat and feedback logging, and controls over what each chat agent is allowed to do. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA -eligible service. This eligibility applies across the Amazon Quick web, desktop, and mobile clients, subject to the shared responsibility model and your configuration. This post, however, focuses on the capabilities of the Amazon Quick web version, which you access through your browser. In this post, we start with the foundations: who HIPAA applies to and the difference between HIPAA-eligible and HIPAA-compliant. We then introduce Amazon Quick as a platform and the two data flows for PHI (unstructured and structured). From there, we cover what Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments and what it doesn’t, walk through a fictional health plan (AnyCompany) deployment, and distill the best practices and irreversible decisions you should make up front. We close with a step-by-step implementation guide, a conclusion, and resources for deeper reading. HIPAA reaches further than hospitals and clinics. Under the law, two categories of organizations carry obligations, and most AI projects touch both. Covered entities and business associates must both sign a business associate addendum (BAA) before PHI changes hands. After you accept the AWS BAA through AWS Artifact, AWS acts as your business associate for that specific AWS account, and only when you use HIPAA-eligible services like Amazon Quick to process PHI within it. The addendum doesn’t extend to your other accounts, to PHI placed in services that are not HIPAA-eligible, or to how you configure the service. Those remain your responsibility. Always review and confirm the current AWS BAA terms and your obligations with your own legal and compliance teams. While HIPAA eligible is an AWS designation, HIPAA compliant is a property of your entire environment. HIPAA eligible means AWS has assessed the service and permits you to use it to process, store, and transmit PHI under a signed AWS BAA. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA-eligible service, and third-party auditors assess it under AWS compliance programs including HIPAA, FedRAMP, PCI DSS, SOC, and ISO. No official HIPAA certification exists for AWS as a cloud service, and AWS itself is not “HIPAA eligible.” Amazon Quick eligibility serves only as a building block. That alone doesn’t make your application and environment HIPAA compliant. You still need to sign the BAA, classify your data, configure the controls correctly, and own the administrative and physical safeguards HIPAA requires, including workforce training, risk analysis, and breach procedures that AWS doesn’t perform for you. The unstructured path runs through knowledge bases, where the documents are controlled by document-level ACLs and evaluated at query time. The structured path runs through Amazon Quick Sight reading your databases and data lakes, where row and column access is controlled by row-level and column-level security. These two data flows carry PHI differently and, as the following section shows, controls are enforced differently in each path. Amazon Quick encrypts data at rest by default and supports encryption for data in transit. They invoke tools, modify data, and interact with external systems on their own. That changes how you approach securing your environment. AWS published four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026, and they apply directly here. Principle 1 — Layer agent safeguards onto your existing security framework. Don’t stand up a parallel security posture for Amazon Quick. Add agent-specific measures (guardrails, topic blocking, and PII redaction) on top of the IAM, network, and encryption policies you already enforce. Principle 2 — Trust deterministic controls over prompt-based ones. A well-crafted adversarial input can circumvent a prompt instruction. Agent instructions are your second layer, not your only one. Register your KMS key first. If your organization requires control of its own encryption keys, register a customer managed key as the account default before creating any Amazon Quick AI resources. The data key is set the first time Quick AI data is created in the account. After that, it can’t be changed. Customer managed key support requires an Enterprise subscription. Note that a customer managed key disables chat memory. Accounts configured with a customer managed key do not support this feature. Choose your identity model deliberately. You have four options: IAM Identity Center, Active Directory, IAM federation, and Quick local users. They differ in provisioning, offboarding, and governance behavior. Inactive-user detection, for instance, works only with IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Switching identity providers after deployment means reprovisioning every user’s permissions and space memberships. Pick once. Make PHI knowledge bases ACL-aware at creation. For supported sources (Amazon S3, Google Drive, SharePoint, Confluence Cloud, and OneDrive), you decide at creation whether a knowledge base enforces document-level ACLs. That setting is permanent. You can’t enable ACLs on a knowledge base that was created without them. For anything PHI-adjacent, create it ACL-aware from the start. Monitor closely: review chat logs weekly, track guardrail trigger rates, and watch access patterns for 30 days after each new workflow goes live. Organizations that build on deterministic, infrastructure-level controls today will likely be well positioned as regulatory expectations catch up to what agentic AI can do.

extraction.body: Protected Health Information (PHI) is any information that identifies a person and relates to their health, care, or payment for care, such as a medical note, a claim, or a member ID. When software touches PHI, it falls under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), the federal law that governs how PHI data is accessed, secured, and audited. Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response. An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further. For example, its chat agents work across both unstructured content, such as clinical notes and appeals letters, and structured data, such as claims and member records.
